name: Question 11
problem:
Find the sum modulo $18$ of the solutions to the congruence $8x≡14\,(\text{mod}\,18).$

*Hint: You may wish to use trial and error to find the appropriate multiplicative inverse.*
worked_solution:
In the given congruence, we have $a=8$ and $n=18$, and so 

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(8,18)=2.
$$

Since $b=14$ is divisible by $2,$ our congruence has $2$ solutions.

First, we use the division property of congruences:

$$
\begin{aligned}8x & ≡14 &  & (\text{mod}\,18) \\ 2\cdot 4x & ≡2\cdot 7 &  & (\text{mod}\,2\cdot 9) \\ \cancel{2}\cdot 4x & ≡\cancel{2}\cdot 7 &  & (\text{mod}\,\cancel{2}\cdot 9) \\ 4x & ≡7 &  & (\text{mod}\,9)\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in this new congruence, we have ${a}_{1}=4$ and ${n}_{1}=9$, where

$$
\text{gcd}({a}_{1},{n}_{1})=\text{gcd}(4,9)=1.
$$

So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $9.$

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $4\,(\text{mod}\,9).$ To find the inverse of $4\,(\text{mod}\,9),$ we compute the exponents of $4\,(\text{mod}\,9)$ until we get a result of $1\,(\text{mod}\,9):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{2} & ≡16≡9+7≡7 &  & (\text{mod}\,9) \\ {4}^{3} & ≡7\cdot 4≡28≡3\cdot 9+1≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,9)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $4\cdot 7≡1\,(\text{mod}\,9),$ which means that $7$ is the multiplicative inverse of $4$ (modulo $9$). 

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & ≡7 &  & (\text{mod}\,9) \\ 7\cdot 4x & ≡7\cdot 7 &  & (\text{mod}\,9) \\ (7\cdot 4)x & ≡49 &  & (\text{mod}\,9) \\ x & ≡49 &  & (\text{mod}\,9) \\ x & ≡5\cdot 9+4 &  & (\text{mod}\,9) \\ x & ≡4 &  & (\text{mod}\,9)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the solution $x≡4\,(\text{mod}\,9).$ 

But our original congruence was modulo $18$ (not modulo $9$). To find all the solutions modulo $18,$ we repeatedly add $9$ modulo $18$ until we reach the number $4$ again:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ≡4 &  & (\text{mod}\,18) \\ {x}_{2} & ≡4+9≡13 &  & (\text{mod}\,18) \\ {x}_{3} & ≡13+9≡22≡1\cdot 18+4≡4≡{x}_{1} &  & (\text{mod}\,18)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x≡4,13\,(\text{mod}\,18).$ 

Finally,

$$
4+13≡17\,(\text{mod}\,18).
$$

EXPLANATION

In the given congruence, we have a=8 and n=18, and so gcd(a,n)=gcd(8,18)=2. Since b=14 is divisible by 2, our congruence has 2 solutions.

First, we use the division property of congruences:

8x≡14(mod18)2⋅4x≡2⋅7(mod2⋅9)2⋅4x≡2⋅7(mod2⋅9)4x≡7(mod9)

Notice that in this new congruence, we have a1=4 and n1=9, where gcd(a1,n1)=gcd(4,9)=1. So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo 9.

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of 4(mod9). To find the inverse of 4(mod9), we compute the exponents of 4(mod9) until we get a result of 1(mod9):

42≡16≡9+7≡7(mod9)43≡7⋅4≡28≡3⋅9+1≡1(mod9)

So, 4⋅7≡1(mod9), which means that 7 is the multiplicative inverse of 4 (modulo 9).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by 7, we get the following:

4x≡7(mod9)7⋅4x≡7⋅7(mod9)(7⋅4)x≡49(mod9)x≡49(mod9)x≡5⋅9+4(mod9)x≡4(mod9)

So, we get the solution x≡4(mod9).

But our original congruence was modulo 18 (not modulo 9). To find all the solutions modulo 18, we repeatedly add 9 modulo 18 until we reach the number 4 again:

x1≡4(mod18)x2≡4+9≡13(mod18)x3≡13+9≡22≡1⋅18+4≡4≡x1(mod18)

Therefore, the solutions are x≡4,13(mod18).

Finally,

4+13≡17(mod18).
